title: Practice in grief
hookLine: in grief, practice may be only breathing: Job's friends sat in silence, and Jewish law frees the fresh mourner from prayer
tomorrow: one disciple refused to believe. why is he still called a saint?

cards: When someone loses a person, the messages pour in: so sorry, here if you need anything, everything happens for a reason. The book of Job has a scene that goes the other way.
Job has lost his children, his wealth, his health. Three friends come to comfort him. When they see him from a distance, they don't recognize him.
They weep. They tear their robes. And then they do the thing they got right.

teach.h: SEVEN DAYS, AND NONE SPAKE A WORD.
teach.b: "So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great." The trouble only starts later, when they begin to explain.
Jewish mourning keeps their first week.
Shiva is the seven days when mourners sit low and visitors come, and tradition says the visitor waits for the mourner to speak first. Jewish law goes further for the rawest hours.

teach.h: THE FRESH MOURNER IS FREED FROM PRAYER.
teach.b: The Mishnah says that someone whose dead still lies before them, not yet buried, is freed from saying the Shema, the daily declaration of faith. For now, the mourner's one task is the person who died.
Later the mourner returns to prayer with the Kaddish, said among others. Here's a neighbor who knows this ground.
In a Buddhist story, Kisa Gotami's little son dies, and she carries him from house to house asking for medicine. The Buddha doesn't argue.

teach.h: KISA GOTAMI AND THE MUSTARD SEED.
teach.b: He asks her for mustard seed from a house where no one has died. Every house has lost someone.
Shared: comfort starts with company, not answers.
One honest difference: Jewish law gives the mourner set days and people around them; Kisa Gotami's road leads to the Buddha's teaching that all things pass, and she becomes a nun.
And if grief ever turns into wanting to die, call or text 988 in the US, or local emergency help anywhere else.

how: Jewish mourners sit shiva, seven days when visitors come to the house, and later say the Kaddish among others; before the burial, Jewish law frees the mourner from some daily prayers. Buddhists tell the story of Kisa Gotami and the mustard seed.

o: when practice shrinks to breathing while others hold the prayers
writing a long speech about the person who has died

games.q: you visit a coworker sitting shiva for her mother. you walk into the living room. what does the tradition suggest you do first?
o: sit down and wait for her to speak first.
tell her right away that her mother is in a better place.
remind her to keep up her daily prayers.
games.why: Job's friends sat in silence for seven days, and at a shiva house tradition says the visitor waits for the mourner to speak.

practice: Let the breath come and go without counting or fixing it. If someone you've lost comes to mind, let them sit with you, the way Job's friends sat, with nothing to say. There's nothing else to do until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Practice in grief: when the practice shrinks to breathing, and others hold the prayers, like Job's friends sitting in silence.

orig.note: Hebrew: seven. the seven days of Jewish mourning, like Job's friends' seven days on the ground.

carryVoice: Your line: just breathing. The friends were best before they said a word. Go gently.
